Chapter 2

Traffic Signs

Road signs, traffic lights and road surface markings — what they mean, which ones override which, and how to read every signal on a Dutch road.

  • General Rules
  • Road Signs
  • Traffic Lights
  • Road Markings

Chapter 2 explains the traffic signs and signals used on Dutch roads. Signs on poles, lights at intersections, lines and symbols painted on the asphalt — all of these are traffic signs in the legal sense, and all of them carry binding instructions for road users.

Understanding how signs work — which ones take priority, how they interact with each other, and what each colour and shape communicates — is as fundamental to the Dutch driving theory exam as the traffic rules themselves.

§ 1 — General Rules for Traffic Signs

The foundational rules that apply to all traffic signs — signs on poles, lights, and markings on the road surface alike.

Obligation to Obey All road users

Every road user must obey all traffic signs that apply to them. This is not optional. A sign displayed according to the rules is legally binding from the moment a road user can reasonably see it.

This obligation applies to the road user themselves — not just to the driver of a vehicle. Pedestrians, cyclists, moped riders, horse riders — all must obey the signs that address them.

Signs Override General Rules Priority of signs

Traffic signs that give an order or prohibition must be obeyed. Where a traffic sign conflicts with a general traffic rule, the traffic sign takes precedence to the extent of that conflict. Traffic lights take precedence over traffic signs that regulate priority. Instructions given by authorised persons take precedence over both traffic signs and traffic rules.

Variable Message Signs Electronic

Electronic signal panels can display legally binding traffic signs and lane-control signals. A red cross above a lane means that lane must not be used. A green arrow means the lane may be used. An electronic A3 speed display gives a maximum speed; if a fixed sign and an electronic panel show different maximum speeds, the lower displayed maximum applies.

A blank matrix sign — one showing nothing — does not change the applicable rules. The default rules and any fixed signs below continue to apply.
Supplementary Boards (Onderborden) Under the sign

A supplementary board is a smaller panel placed directly below a traffic sign. It modifies, limits or clarifies the main sign. For example, a no-parking sign may have a supplementary board showing specific hours during which parking is prohibited — outside those hours, parking is permitted. Always read supplementary boards as part of the main sign instruction.

Where Signs Apply Scope of a sign

A traffic sign generally applies from the point where it is placed. Signs for a road apply to the entire carriageway in the direction indicated. Some signs apply only to the lane above which they are positioned — this is the case for matrix signs on motorways. Supplementary boards can further define the zone of application.

When Instructions Conflict

Use the legal precedence rules, not an oversimplified universal ladder.

Authorised-person instructions override traffic signs and traffic rules
›
Traffic lights override priority signs
›
Traffic signs override incompatible general traffic rules

§ 2 — Road Signs (Verkeersborden)

Dutch road signs are organised into categories by letter code. Shape and colour communicate the type of instruction before you even read the detail.

How Dutch Signs Are Organised

Every Dutch road sign belongs to a lettered category. The category tells you immediately what kind of instruction the sign carries. Learning the categories is one of the most efficient ways to prepare for the theory exam — once you know the system, individual signs become much easier to recognise and remember.

CategoryNameShape & colourWhat it does
ASpeedSpeed-limit and advisory-speed signsA1 = maximum speed; A2 = end of maximum speed; A3 = maximum speed on an electronic display; A4 = advisory speed; A5 = end of advisory speed
BPriorityVarious distinctive shapesPriority roads and priority at junctions. B6 = give priority; B7 = stop and give priority
CRoad closures / access restrictionsMostly red-bordered restriction signs, plus one-way/access signsControls access by direction, vehicle type, dimensions, weight and certain zones
DPositive instructionsBlue circular signs with white arrowsCompulsory direction of travel and passing side
EParking and stoppingMostly blue signs with parking/stopping symbolsE1 = no parking; E2 = no stopping; E4 = parking area; other E-signs regulate designated parking
FOther ordersVariousIncludes overtaking restrictions, priority over/oncoming traffic, no U-turns and stop instructions
GTraffic regulations / road typesMostly blue rectangular or circular signsMotorway, autoweg, erf, footpath, bridleway and cycle-path designations
HBuilt-up areaPlace-name signsH1 = start of built-up area; H2 = end of built-up area
JWarning signsRed-bordered trianglesWarns of hazards such as bends, crossings, roadworks, slippery roads and queues
KDirection signsDirection and destination panelsRoute, destination, exit and diversion information
LInformation signsMostly rectangular information signsIncludes pedestrian crossings, stops, lane information, tunnels, hard shoulders and emergency facilities

Priority Signs — Category B

Priority signs are among the most critical on Dutch roads. They define who has the right of way at intersections and junctions.

B1
Priority road — you have right of way
B2
End of priority road
B3
Priority crossroads — you have priority at the junction
B4
Priority junction — side road from the left
B6
Give way — yield to crossing traffic
B7
Stop — come to a full stop before proceeding
B6 vs B7 — Give Way vs Stop

The B6 (give way) requires you to yield — slow down, check, and proceed only if safe. You do not have to stop if the way is clear. The B7 (stop) requires a complete stop — you must come to a full standstill before the stop line, regardless of whether traffic is present. Failing to make a full stop at a B7 is a violation even if no other vehicle is visible.

Prohibition Signs — Category C

C1
Road closed in both directions to vehicles, riders and persons in charge of animals or livestock
C2
No entry in this direction
C6
No access for vehicles with more than two wheels
C7
No access for goods vehicles
C11
No access for motorcycles
C12
No access for motor vehicles
C16
No access for pedestrians
C22
No access for vehicles carrying hazardous substances

Other Orders — Categories E & F

E1
No parking
E2
No stopping
F1
No overtaking
F5
Give way to oncoming vehicles
F6
Priority over oncoming vehicles
F7

Obligation Signs — Category D

Obligation signs are blue circles with white symbols. They tell you what you must do — not what you must avoid.

D1
Roundabout — compulsory direction of travel
D2
Pass the sign on the side indicated by the arrow
D3
The sign may be passed on either side
D4
Drive ahead only
D5
Follow the direction shown by the arrow
D6
Follow one of the directions shown by the arrows

G1
Start of motorway (autosnelweg)
G2
End of motorway
G3
Start of expressway (autoweg)
G4
End of expressway
G5
Start of erf (home zone / living street)
G6
End of erf
G7
Footpath
G8
End of footpath
G11
Mandatory bicycle path

Combined bicycle/moped path

Optional (non-mandatory) bicycle path

Warning Signs — Category J

Warning signs are triangles with a red border. They alert you to a hazard ahead. They do not prohibit anything — they ask you to be prepared and adjust your speed and attention.

J2
Dangerous right-hand bend ahead
J8
Dangerous crossing ahead
J12
Level crossing with single track
J13
Level crossing with two or more tracks
J15
Opening or swing bridge ahead
J16
School crossing ahead
J21
School crossing ahead
J22
Pedestrian crossing ahead
J33
Queues likely
Reading Warning Signs Correctly

Warning signs do not change your right of way or prohibit any action. They warn you to prepare. When you see a J-sign, reduce speed, increase following distance, and be ready for the hazard described. The sign tells you what is coming — it is your job to respond appropriately.

Speed Limit Signs — Ending a Limit

A2 — End of Speed Limit

A2 marks the end of the maximum speed shown by an A1 sign. After A2, determine the applicable speed from the road type, other signs and any electronic signals. Do not automatically assume 130 km/h on a motorway; Dutch motorway limits can vary by location and time of day.

A4 — Advisory Speed

A square sign (not round) with a speed number is an advisory speed — recommended, not mandatory. It typically appears before a sharp bend or road narrowing. You are not breaking the law by going faster, but the advisory exists for a reason.

§ 3 — Traffic Lights (Verkeerslichten)

What each light colour and combination means — and what you must do when you see it.

Obligation to Obey Traffic Lights All road users

Traffic lights are legally binding. Every road user must follow the instruction of the light that applies to them. Running a red light is one of the most serious traffic violations and is a common cause of fatal accidents at intersections.

If traffic lights are not functioning — showing nothing at all — the general traffic rules apply, including the give-way-to-the-right rule at intersections.

Standard Vehicle Traffic Lights

Red — Stop
Come to a full stop before the stop line. Do not proceed under any circumstances.
Green — Proceed
You may proceed, but still give way to pedestrians and cyclists already crossing.
Yellow — Stop if safe
Stop before the line if you can do so safely. Only proceed if stopping would be dangerous.
→
Green Arrow — Direction-specific green
The green signal applies only to the direction shown by the arrow. Proceed only in that direction and continue to observe any duties that still apply.
Flashing Yellow — Danger / caution
A flashing yellow light means danger: take care. Follow the traffic rules and any other applicable signs.
Yellow Light — The Most Misunderstood Signal

Yellow does not mean accelerate. It means stop — if you can do so safely. The exception is if stopping would require sudden harsh braking that could cause a rear-end collision or other danger. Only in that case may you continue through yellow.

Green — Not Unconditional

A green light permits you to proceed — but it does not remove your obligation to give way. When a light turns green, you must still yield to pedestrians who are crossing and cyclists who are on the crossing. Green means proceed, but you must still avoid endangering or obstructing road users who are lawfully in your path.

Pedestrian Traffic Lights

Red figure — Do not cross
Wait at the kerb. Do not step onto the crossing.
Green figure — Cross now
Cross promptly. If the green starts flashing, complete the crossing — do not start if you are not yet on the road.
Flashing green figure — Hurry
Finish crossing. Do not start crossing if you have not yet stepped off the kerb.

Bicycle Traffic Lights

Bicycle-Specific Lights Fietsers

Where a separate traffic light for cyclists is present — recognisable by the bicycle symbol on the light housing — cyclists must follow that light, not the general vehicle light. The same red/yellow/green rules apply.

Cyclists must follow the traffic light that applies to their direction and road position. Where an illuminated bicycle symbol is shown, that signal specifically applies to cyclists, mopeds on a cycle/moped track and drivers of disabled persons' vehicles.

A plate reading “Right turn clear for bicycles” or “Right turn clear for bicycles and mopeds” can make the red and amber lights inapplicable to the indicated road users turning right; they must then give way to other road users.

Tram & Bus Lights

Public Transport Traffic Lights Trams & buses

Trams and scheduled buses can be controlled by dedicated signals. For these signals, white or flashing white means proceed in the direction indicated, amber means stop unless stopping safely can no longer reasonably be expected, and red means stop. The signals also apply to other vehicles using a bus lane where that signal applies.

Matrix Signs Above Motorway Lanes

Lane Signals on Motorways Per-lane control

On Dutch motorways, electronic matrix signs above each lane control that specific lane individually. The possible signals are:

  • Green arrow pointing down — lane is open, you may use it
  • Red cross (X) — lane is closed, you must not drive in it
  • White arrow — advance warning that a red cross is coming; move out of the lane as indicated
  • Speed limit number — the displayed A3 maximum speed applies
A matrix sign overrides the general speed limit for that lane. If a fixed sign and an electronic panel show different maximum speeds, the lower displayed maximum applies.

§ 4 — Road Surface Markings

Lines, symbols and patterns on the road surface — what each one means and how to respond to it.

Road Markings Are Binding Legal force

Road markings can impose binding rules where the RVV gives them a legal meaning. Important examples include continuous lines, hatched areas (verdrijvingsvlakken), lane-direction arrows, stop lines, shark's teeth and BUS/LIJNBUS lanes. Their exact effect depends on the type of marking and the applicable rule.

Lane Lines

Continuous White Line — Lane Boundary

A solid continuous white line between lanes may not be crossed. This applies to the centre line between opposing traffic directions and to lane-dividing lines marked as continuous. You must stay on your side.

Broken White Line — May Cross

A broken (dashed) white line marks a lane boundary that may be crossed when safe to do so — for example, when overtaking or changing lanes. You must still check that it is safe before crossing.

Double Continuous Line

A double continuous line contains a continuous line for traffic on both sides. The normal rule for continuous lines applies, including the specific statutory exceptions.

Continuous + Broken Combination

When a continuous line runs alongside a broken line, the rule depends on which side you are on. If the continuous line is on your side, you may not cross. If the broken line is on your side, you may cross when safe. Look at the line closest to you.

Stop and Give-Way Lines

Stop Line (Stopstreep)

A thick continuous white line across the road at a traffic light or stop sign. You must stop with the front of your vehicle behind this line. When you are required to stop, stop behind the stop line.

Give-Way Line (Haaientanden)

Shark's teeth — rows of triangles pointing toward you — indicate a give-way obligation. You must yield to traffic on the road you are about to enter. Often found at roundabouts and at junctions where a B6 sign is also present.

Pedestrian & Cyclist Crossings

Zebra Crossing (Voetgangersoversteekplaats)

Parallel white stripes across the road. Drivers must give way to pedestrians who are on the crossing or who are clearly about to step onto it. A zebra crossing gives the statutory protection to pedestrians and drivers of disabled persons' vehicles. A bicycle symbol by itself does not automatically give cyclists the same priority; check the priority signs and shark's teeth.

Cyclist Crossing (Fietsoversteekplaats)

Marked with two broken white lines across the road and a bicycle symbol. A cycle crossing marking by itself does not determine priority. Check B-signs, shark's teeth and the general priority rules to determine who must give way.

Special Marked Zones on the Road Surface

Block Markings (Blokmarkering)

A pattern of white blocks separates an entry or exit lane from the main carriageway. Driving over block markings is not automatically prohibited, but they indicate a transition zone — treat with care.

Diversion Area (Verdrijvingsvlak)

An area covered with diagonal stripes. Driving on this is prohibited. It is used to steer traffic away from an obstacle or to separate opposing streams. Treat it as solid ground you must not enter.

Junction Point (Puntstuk)

A triangular or polygonal marked area at a point where lanes split or merge. Do not drive on it and do not stop on it. It is a visual guide to keep traffic separated at complex junctions.

Yellow Lines — Stopping Restrictions

A continuous yellow line along the edge of the carriageway means no stopping. A broken yellow line means no parking. These Dutch markings should not be confused with yellow-line systems used in some other countries.

BUS / LIJNBUS Text

A bus lane marked BUS may be used by scheduled buses, coaches and trams. A lane marked LIJNBUS may be used by scheduled buses and trams. Other use requires a separate legal basis or exemption.

Bicycle Symbol on Carriageway

A bicycle symbol together with the lane marking identifies a bicycle lane (fietsstrook). Do not treat a broken border as general permission for motor vehicles to drive in the cycle lane; the rules for road position and the specific marking still apply.

Continuous vs Broken — The Key Distinction

For ordinary lane boundaries, a continuous line generally may not be crossed, subject to specific statutory exceptions; a broken line can be crossed when the manoeuvre is otherwise permitted and safe. Do not extend that shortcut to every road marking: cycle lanes, bus lanes, hatched areas and other markings have their own rules.

Arrow Markings on the Road

Direction Arrows Lane guidance

Arrows painted on the road surface inside a lane indicate the permitted direction(s) for that lane. If an arrow points straight ahead, you must go straight. If it shows a right turn, you must turn right. If your intended direction differs from the arrow, you must change lanes before the arrow.

Arrows are often combined with text (e.g. "BUS" or a lane number) to further clarify the permitted use of that lane.

Speed Limit Markings On the road surface

Speed numbers are sometimes painted on the road surface as reminders or visual reinforcement. A painted number by itself is not the same as an A1 maximum-speed sign. Determine the legally applicable maximum speed from the traffic signs, electronic signals and the general speed rules.

Chapter 2 — What to Take Away

Dutch traffic signs and signals include the A–L sign categories, traffic lights, electronic signals and legally defined road markings. Instructions from authorised persons take precedence over traffic signs and traffic rules; traffic lights take precedence over signs that regulate priority; traffic signs take precedence over incompatible general traffic rules. Shark's teeth require drivers to give priority to crossing drivers. A red X above a lane means that lane must not be used.

For the exam, focus especially on: the B6/B7 distinction (give way vs full stop), the meaning of yellow at traffic lights, direction-specific green signals, matrix signs on motorways, and the difference between solid and broken bicycle lane borders.
